notes.meaning: Jeremiah is still praying. He admits that Israel entered the good land God gave them, but then refused to listen to God's voice or follow His law. They could not claim they didn't know better, because God had made His will clear. So the disaster now falling on them is not bad luck. It is the fair result of their sin.

The enemy army has piled up earth ramps against the walls. They used these to bring their battering machines close to the city. Inside, hunger and disease are wearing the people down. Everything God warned about through His prophets is coming true. Jeremiah takes comfort that God sees it all and knows how to fix it.

Here is what puzzles Jeremiah. God told him to buy a field, even though the city is about to fall to the Babylonians (the "Chaldeans"). Jeremiah obeyed right away. Now he asks God to help him understand why. We should never argue with God's commands, but it is right to ask what they mean.

God answers by handing Jeremiah's own words from verse 17 back to him: nothing is too hard for God. "God of all flesh" means the God on whom every human life depends. Here "flesh" stresses how weak people are. No one can block God's plans, whether He is judging or restoring. So bringing His people back to the land will not be hard for Him either.

God has not changed His mind. Jerusalem will still fall to Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. A promise of future mercy does not cancel the trouble coming now. What God said through Jeremiah will come true.

The invaders will burn the city. That includes the houses where people burned incense to Baal on their flat rooftops. They burned incense there, so their houses will be burned. They did these things openly and on purpose, as if daring God to be angry.

From the nation's "youth" in the wilderness after leaving Egypt, the people kept doing evil. The wording points to a steady habit, not a single slip. "The work of their hands" points to the idols they made and the worship they invented for themselves.

From its early days, Jerusalem kept stirring up God's anger. It turned to idols as early as Solomon's reign. Now the time has come to remove it. Every level of society shared the guilt: kings, officials, priests, prophets and ordinary people. Even when leaders and ministers fall away, God's people are still called to stay faithful.

Turning your back on someone who is speaking is a sign of contempt. God taught His people through the prophets "again and again" (literally, "rising up early"). He was like a caring parent who gets up early to teach a child. Yet they would not listen or accept correction.

The worst insult was putting idols inside God's own temple, the house that bore His name. They worshipped false gods not only on hills and in groves but right in God's house. That made the holy place unclean.

In the Valley of Hinnom they built altars to Baal and offered their own children to the god Molech. God says He never commanded this, and it never even entered His mind. Good intentions are no excuse. Worship God has not asked for is not pleasing to Him. This evil spread and led the whole land into sin.

Now the message turns: "But now, nevertheless." The people had laughed off God's warnings. Now they swung to the other extreme and gave up all hope. Yet God, for the sake of His covenant (His binding promise), speaks hope into that despair.

God promises to gather His scattered people from every land and bring them home to live in safety. He had promised this long before through Moses. The exile would only be for a time. Calvin notes that the return from Babylon did not bring full safety, so the promise reaches further, to the kingdom of Christ.

differ.view: The return from Babylon was only a first taste. The promise is fully kept in Christ's kingdom, where believers are planted in His church.
Because it says "all the lands," and lasting safety never came after Babylon, this points to a future gathering of Israel to its land.

notes.meaning: This is the old covenant promise heard since Exodus: "They will be My people, and I will be their God." It is the best blessing of all, better than wealth or comfort. God gives Himself to them, and all He is and has works for their good.

God promises to give them a single, undivided heart and one way of life, so that they always honor Him. Only God can change a heart like this, by making people new through His Spirit. They will also be united with each other in the great truths of the faith. This brings good to them and to their children after them.

This "everlasting covenant" is the same new covenant promised in chapter 31. God promises two things. He will never stop doing them good, and He will put reverence for Him in their hearts so they will not turn away. Staying faithful to the end comes from God's grace, not from our own strength.

God says He will be glad to do them good, the way a loving father enjoys blessing his children. He uses human words like "heart" and "soul" so that we can understand Him. He will plant them firmly and faithfully, never to be pulled up again.

God has kept His warnings, so He will surely keep His promises too. The disaster came just as He said, and the good will come just as surely. The return from Babylon was only a small foretaste of the grace God would give through Christ.

Now God explains Jeremiah's field. One day people will again buy land, with proper deeds, signatures and witnesses, all over the country. Benjamin is named first because Jeremiah's field at Anathoth lay there. His purchase was a pledge that God would bring His people home and restore what they had lost. Henry adds that these fields are a faint picture of the lasting home in heaven kept for all who fear God.
